Getting started with BiHeat

Source: vignettes/biheat.Rmd
biheat.Rmd

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("gcol33/BiHeat")
library(BiHeat)

Two matrices, one plot

BiHeat draws a heatmap where every cell is cut along a diagonal. The upper triangle carries a value from one matrix, the lower triangle carries the value from the same position in a second matrix.

Here are species occurrence probabilities across sites, observed and predicted by some model:

set.seed(1)
species   <- LETTERS[1:6]
sites     <- letters[1:8]
observed  <- matrix(runif(48), 6, 8, dimnames = list(species, sites))
predicted <- observed + matrix(rnorm(48, sd = 0.15), 6, 8,
                               dimnames = list(species, sites))

biheat(observed, predicted)

Each cell holds both numbers at once. A cell whose two halves are similarly pale, or similarly saturated, is a cell where the model agreed with the data. A cell with a deep half against a washed-out half is a cell where it did not. The comparison happens inside one cell, at the resolution of a single species at a single site, without the eye travelling between two panels.

The pairing generalises past observed and predicted. Mean and variance, correlation and p-value, train and test accuracy, model A and model B, richness before and after: any two numeric matrices sharing a shape are candidates.

Reading a split cell

Three things carry information in the panel, and it helps to know which one you are reading.

Within a single cell, the contrast between the two halves is the comparison. A cell whose halves differ sharply is a disagreement between the two matrices at that row and column. This is the reading the split makes cheap, because both values occupy one spot and the eye needs no saccade between panels.

Down a column or across a row, the variation within one triangle is the gradient of that matrix. The upper triangles of a row read as a small heatmap of their own, and so do the lower ones.

Across the two palettes, colour is a label rather than a quantity. Red and blue carry no relative meaning, so a saturated red half and a saturated blue half say that both values are high in their own matrix, not that they are equal.

That last point is where scale matters. Under the default "separate", each triangle spans its own range, so the halves of a cell cannot be compared as numbers, only as positions within their own matrix. Under "shared" they span one range and a visible mismatch inside a cell is a real numeric difference.

The diagonal direction changes which halves sit next to each other. With split = "down" the upper triangles of horizontally adjacent cells meet across the cell boundary, which favours reading along rows. split = "up" favours reading down columns. Neither changes the data, and switching between them is worth doing when the panel is meant to support one direction of comparison.

biheat(observed, predicted, split = "up")

The clutch

biheat() renders in one call. Underneath it runs a three-stage lifecycle that you can also drive yourself, and the object in the middle of it carries more than the two matrices.

clutch <- breed(observed, predicted)
clutch
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: observed (6 x 8)
#>   lower: predicted (6 x 8)
#>   align: intersect  (6 rows x 8 cols kept)
#>   cells: 48 finite / 48 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: 0.911   rmse: 0.136   mae: 0.104

breed() returns a clutch. It aligned the two matrices, counted the usable cells, and computed the comparison statistics that the print method reports: Pearson and Spearman correlation, RMSE, and MAE. Those sit in clutch$meta alongside the value range of each side:

str(clutch$meta)
#> List of 10
#>  $ n_cells     : int 48
#>  $ n_finite    : int 48
#>  $ n_na        : int 0
#>  $ upper_range : num [1:2] 0.0134 0.9919
#>  $ lower_range : num [1:2] -0.000584 1.154483
#>  $ shared_range: num [1:2] -0.000584 1.154483
#>  $ pearson     : num 0.911
#>  $ spearman    : num 0.914
#>  $ rmse        : num 0.136
#>  $ mae         : num 0.104

Nothing about the drawing has happened yet. A clutch is the paired data plus what BiHeat learned about the pair, which makes it worth keeping around even when the plot is not the immediate goal:

round(clutch$meta$spearman, 3)
#> [1] 0.914
round(clutch$meta$rmse, 3)
#> [1] 0.136

Anything as.matrix() can turn into a numeric matrix is accepted, so a pair of all-numeric data frames needs no conversion first:

breed(as.data.frame(observed), as.data.frame(predicted))
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: as.data.frame(observed) (6 x 8)
#>   lower: as.data.frame(predicted) (6 x 8)
#>   align: intersect  (6 rows x 8 cols kept)
#>   cells: 48 finite / 48 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: 0.911   rmse: 0.136   mae: 0.104

A non-numeric input stops the call rather than coercing silently:

breed(matrix(letters[1:6], 2, 3), matrix(1:6, 2, 3))
#> Error:
#> ! `a` must be a numeric matrix.

The labels on the legend come from the symbols you passed in. breed(observed, predicted) recorded "observed" and "predicted" by reading the call, so the two colourbars name themselves. Pass upper_name and lower_name when the variables are called something less presentable.

breed(observed, predicted,
      upper_name = "field survey",
      lower_name = "model fit")
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: field survey (6 x 8)
#>   lower: model fit (6 x 8)
#>   align: intersect  (6 rows x 8 cols kept)
#>   cells: 48 finite / 48 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: 0.911   rmse: 0.136   mae: 0.104

How the two matrices get aligned

Two matrices that came from different pipelines rarely arrive with their rows and columns in the same order, or even with the same rows and columns. breed() handles that before anything is drawn, so a mismatch shows up as a message about your data rather than as a plot that quietly compares the wrong cells.

The default, align = "intersect", works on dimnames. When both matrices carry row names, BiHeat keeps the rows present in both; the same rule applies to columns.

a <- matrix(runif(12), 3, 4,
            dimnames = list(c("x", "y", "z"), c("s1", "s2", "s3", "s4")))
b <- matrix(runif(12), 3, 4,
            dimnames = list(c("y", "z", "w"), c("s2", "s3", "s4", "s5")))

breed(a, b)
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: a (2 x 3)
#>   lower: b (2 x 3)
#>   align: intersect  (2 rows x 3 cols kept)
#>   dropped: 2 rows, 2 cols
#>   cells: 6 finite / 6 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: -0.821   rmse: 0.463   mae: 0.376

Two rows and two columns went away, and the clutch says so. The detail of which labels were dropped, and from which side, sits in align_report:

str(breed(a, b)$align_report)
#> List of 7
#>  $ mode          : chr "intersect"
#>  $ rows_kept     : int 2
#>  $ cols_kept     : int 3
#>  $ rows_dropped_a: chr "x"
#>  $ rows_dropped_b: chr "w"
#>  $ cols_dropped_a: chr "s1"
#>  $ cols_dropped_b: chr "s5"

An axis where only one matrix carries names, or where neither does, is matched by position instead, which requires the two lengths to agree. align = "by_position" skips the name logic entirely and pairs cell [i, j] with cell [i, j]:

u <- matrix(runif(6), 2, 3)
l <- matrix(runif(6), 2, 3)
breed(u, l, align = "by_position")
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: u (2 x 3)
#>   lower: l (2 x 3)
#>   align: by_position  (2 rows x 3 cols kept)
#>   cells: 6 finite / 6 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: -0.676   rmse: 0.357   mae: 0.296

Two failures stop the call rather than guessing. Matrices of different shapes with no names to align on:

breed(matrix(1:6, 2, 3), matrix(1:12, 3, 4))
#> Error:
#> ! Matrices have different dimensions (2x3 vs 3x4); cannot align by position.

And named matrices whose names have nothing in common:

breed(
  matrix(1:6, 2, 3, dimnames = list(c("a", "b"), c("x", "y", "z"))),
  matrix(1:6, 2, 3, dimnames = list(c("c", "d"), c("x", "y", "z")))
)
#> Error:
#> ! No overlapping row names between `a` and `b`.

Missing cells

A gap in one matrix belongs to one triangle. BiHeat keeps the cell, draws the half it has, and fills the missing half with na_colour:

observed_gaps <- observed
observed_gaps[2, 3] <- NA
observed_gaps[5, 7] <- NA

gappy <- breed(observed_gaps, predicted)
gappy
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: observed_gaps (6 x 8)
#>   lower: predicted (6 x 8)
#>   align: intersect  (6 rows x 8 cols kept)
#>   cells: 46 finite / 48 total (2 NA)
#>   pearson: 0.913   rmse: 0.138   mae: 0.106

The cell count separates the two quantities: 48 cells exist, and the number reported as finite is how many have a value on both sides. The correlation, RMSE, and MAE use that subset. Two grey half-cells appear in the panel:

plot(gappy, na_colour = "grey85")

Separate and shared colour scales

Each triangle gets its own colour range by default, which is what you want when the two matrices measure different things. A correlation matrix paired with the p-values of those correlations is the clearest case: one side lives on [-1, 1], the other on [0, 1], and forcing them onto a common range would waste most of both palettes.

set.seed(42)
m <- matrix(rnorm(200), 40, 5, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("v", 1:5)))
m[, 2] <- m[, 1] * 0.8 + rnorm(40, sd = 0.6)
m[, 4] <- m[, 3] * -0.5 + rnorm(40, sd = 0.8)

cmat <- cor(m)
pmat <- outer(seq_len(5), seq_len(5),
              Vectorize(function(i, j) stats::cor.test(m[, i], m[, j])$p.value))
dimnames(pmat) <- dimnames(cmat)

biheat(cmat, pmat, upper_name = "correlation", lower_name = "p-value")

scale = "shared" puts both triangles on one range, which is what makes a cross-triangle comparison mean something. Observed against predicted qualifies, since both are probabilities in the same units:

biheat(observed, predicted, scale = "shared")

The choice changes the reading of the same data. Under "separate", each side is stretched across its own minimum and maximum, so a pale upper half means low relative to the other observed values. Under "shared", the same pale half means low relative to everything in both matrices, and a visible difference between the two halves of one cell is a real difference in probability. The observed and predicted matrices here differ by 0.136 RMSE, which is small enough that the shared version looks close to symmetric.

The lifecycle

biheat(observed, predicted, scale = "shared") is sugar. Written out, it is:

breed(observed, predicted) |>
  incubate(scale = "shared") |>
  plot()

incubate() records rendering options on the clutch and hands it back, so calls layer the way ggplot2’s + does. Splitting one call into several changes nothing:

breed(observed, predicted) |>
  incubate(scale = "shared") |>
  incubate(split = "up") |>
  incubate(show_values = TRUE, value_size = 2.4) |>
  plot()

Options are stored, not validated on the spot, so a partial configuration is allowed to exist. Validation happens when plot() reads the config:

breed(observed, predicted) |>
  incubate(scale = "sheared") |>
  plot()
#> Error in `match.arg()`:
#> ! 'arg' should be one of "separate", "shared"

A configured clutch prints its config, which is a quick way to see what a long pipeline has accumulated:

breed(observed, predicted) |>
  incubate(scale = "shared", split = "up", show_values = TRUE)
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: observed (6 x 8)
#>   lower: predicted (6 x 8)
#>   align: intersect  (6 rows x 8 cols kept)
#>   cells: 48 finite / 48 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: 0.911   rmse: 0.136   mae: 0.104
#>   config: scale=shared, split=up, show_values=TRUE

plot() takes rendering options too, treating them as one final incubate() pass. These three lines draw the same figure:

biheat(observed, predicted, split = "up")
breed(observed, predicted) |> incubate(split = "up") |> plot()
breed(observed, predicted) |> plot(split = "up")

Verbs

Four verbs take a clutch and return a clutch, which is what lets them chain.

switch_sides() exchanges the two matrices, along with their names and ranges. straighten() flips the diagonal between "down" and "up". bothways() toggles between separate and shared scales, or takes the value outright.

breed(observed, predicted) |>
  switch_sides() |>
  straighten() |>
  bothways() |>
  plot()

predicted is now on top, the diagonal runs the other way, and the scale is shared. Each verb reads the current state and moves it one step, so calling bothways() twice returns to where it started:

breed(observed, predicted) |> bothways() |> bothways()
#> <clutch>
#>   upper: observed (6 x 8)
#>   lower: predicted (6 x 8)
#>   align: intersect  (6 rows x 8 cols kept)
#>   cells: 48 finite / 48 total (0 NA)
#>   pearson: 0.911   rmse: 0.136   mae: 0.104
#>   config: scale=separate

comes_out() goes the other direction and returns the per-cell table:

cells <- comes_out(breed(observed, predicted))
head(cells)
#> <biheat_data> 6 cells (6 x 8)
#>   upper = observed
#>   lower = predicted
#>   row col i j     upper     lower
#> 1   A   a 1 1 0.2655087 0.3584825
#> 2   B   a 2 1 0.3721239 0.3637046
#> 3   C   a 3 1 0.5728534 0.5494840
#> 4   D   a 4 1 0.9082078 0.6875949
#> 5   E   a 5 1 0.2016819 0.1299594
#> 6   F   a 6 1 0.8983897 0.9610809

One row per cell, with the matrix indices, the labels, and both values. That table is what geom_biheat() consumes, and it is a convenient starting point for questions the heatmap is not the right shape for:

cells$error <- cells$lower - cells$upper
head(cells[order(-abs(cells$error)), c("row", "col", "upper", "lower", "error")], 4)
#> <biheat_data> 4 cells (0 x 0)
#>   upper = 
#>   lower = 
#>    row col     upper     lower      error
#> 37   A   g 0.7942399 1.1544825  0.3602427
#> 46   D   h 0.7893562 1.1152480  0.3258918
#> 32   B   f 0.5995658 0.8966258  0.2970600
#> 43   A   h 0.7829328 0.5121890 -0.2707438

comes_out() also accepts a plot that BiHeat drew, so the data is recoverable from the figure:

p <- biheat(observed, predicted)
identical(comes_out(p), comes_out(breed(observed, predicted)))
#> [1] TRUE

What plot() hands back

The default return is a biheat_plot, a gtable holding the panel and the paired legend with its split-tile key glyph:

class(biheat(observed, predicted))
#> [1] "biheat_plot" "gtable"      "gTree"       "grob"        "gDesc"

It prints like any plot and ggplot2::ggsave() accepts it. ggplot2’s + works on ggplot objects, and a gtable is not one, so adding a component to a rendered BiHeat plot returns NULL:

class(biheat(observed, predicted) + ggplot2::labs(title = "observed vs predicted"))
#> [1] "NULL"

That is how ggplot2 treats any gtable, including one from ggplot2::ggplotGrob(). Titles, labels, and every other rendering option go through incubate() or the ... of biheat() instead:

biheat(observed, predicted,
       title = "Occurrence probability",
       subtitle = "field survey against model fit",
       caption = "48 cells, 6 species x 8 sites")

Turning the key glyph off leaves nothing to inject, and the underlying ggplot comes back instead. That object does take +:

p_gg <- biheat(observed, predicted, show_key = FALSE)
class(p_gg)
#> [1] "ggplot2::ggplot" "ggplot"          "ggplot2::gg"     "S7_object"      
#> [5] "gg"

p_gg + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Sizing the panel

The legend column holds two colourbars and the key glyph at fixed centimetre sizes, and measures about 4.65 cm whatever the figure dimensions. The panel takes what is left, so the width available for cells is the figure width minus that column and the axis labels.

A 7 inch wide figure is 17.8 cm, leaving roughly 12 cm of panel. Spread over 8 columns that is 1.5 cm per cell, and over 30 columns it is 4 mm, at which point a cell is a pair of small triangles and the tick labels have started to overlap. Two ways to buy width back:

# move the legend under the panel
biheat(observed, predicted, legend_position = "bottom")

# drop the key glyph, keeping the colourbars
biheat(observed, predicted, show_key = FALSE)

show_values = TRUE needs considerably more room, since two numbers have to fit inside one cell. It stays legible to roughly 8 columns at the default figure width. Lowering value_size fits a few more columns in, at smaller type.

When the split cell works

The design assumes the two matrices are worth looking at together, cell by cell. Cases where it earns its place:

  • The two matrices are the same measurement under two conditions, and the question is where they disagree. Observed against predicted, before against after, two models scored on one grid.
  • One matrix qualifies the other, as a correlation does with its p-value, so each cell is a value plus its trustworthiness.
  • The grid is small enough that individual cells are meant to be read. Up to a few hundred cells the split is legible; past that the panel reads as texture and two side-by-side heatmaps show the broad pattern more directly.

Cases where something else fits better:

  • Three or more matrices. The cell has two halves, and a facet over a long table handles the rest.

  • One matrix, where a plain ggplot2::geom_tile() is simpler.

  • Matrices whose interesting structure is the ordering itself, where a clustered heatmap with dendrograms does work BiHeat does not attempt.

The comparison statistics on the clutch are a check on the last point. A pair with a Pearson correlation near 1 and a small RMSE will draw as an almost symmetric panel, and the figure then has little to show:

c(pearson = round(clutch$meta$pearson, 3),
  rmse    = round(clutch$meta$rmse, 3),
  mae     = round(clutch$meta$mae, 3))
#> pearson    rmse     mae 
#>   0.911   0.136   0.104
